issues.legal_issue: A subordinate court’s order cannot be challenged in a later constitutional writ proceeding after a superior court has decided a civil revision concerning that same order after hearing the parties.
material_facts: A party challenged a trial court’s order in an appeal, and the appellate court made an order concerning possession of rented premises.

The party sought revision of the appellate order under the Civil Procedure Code, and a single judge dismissed the revision after considering whether the appellate court had acted illegally or with material irregularity.
The party then brought a writ petition under Articles 226 and 227 challenging the same appellate order.
The division bench allowed the writ petition and set aside the orders of the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The appellate order merged in the High Court’s order on revision and could not be attacked through a separate writ petition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, revision is a mode of exercising the High Court’s superior review jurisdiction, and the principle of merger is not inapplicable merely because the jurisdiction is revisional rather than appellate. The Court relied on Madan Lal Rungta v. Secretary to the Government of Orissa; Nagendra Nath Dey v. Suresh Chandra Dey; Raja of Ramnad v. Kamid Rowthen; P.P.P. Chidambara Nadar v. C.P.A. Rama Nadar; Secretary of State for India in Council v. British India Steam Navigation Company; U.J.S. Chopra v. State of Bombay; and Chandi Prasad Chokhani v. State of Bihar. It rejected the contrary approach in K.B. Sipahimalani v. Fidahussein Vallibhoy.

predicates.civil_revision_followed_by_writ: A party first sought revision of a subordinate court’s order in a civil proceeding and later brought a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.revision_decided_after_hearing: The superior court decided the revision after hearing the parties.
predicates.later_writ_attacks_same_order: The later writ proceeding challenges the same order that was the subject of the revision.

issues.definition: When a party brings a writ proceeding against the same subordinate order after a superior court has decided a civil revision concerning it after hearing the parties, the subordinate order merges in the revision order.

issues.legal_issue: A party that has chosen and exhausted revision cannot properly obtain relief through a later writ proceeding against the same subordinate court order, even if merger does not apply.
material_facts: The party challenged the appellate court’s order by filing a revision petition, which the High Court dismissed.
The party then invoked Articles 226 and 227 to challenge that same appellate order.
The division bench entertained the writ petition and set aside the lower courts’ orders, creating a conflict with the earlier decision in the revision proceeding.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the appellate order had not merged in the revision order, the High Court ought not to have entertained the writ petition after the party had chosen and exhausted revision against the same order.
issues.legal_principle: The exercise of writ and supervisory jurisdiction is discretionary. Where a party has chosen and exhausted one available mode of invoking the High Court’s jurisdiction against an order, granting relief in another proceeding against that same order is not a proper exercise of discretion; refusing relief helps prevent abuse of process and preserves finality and consistency of decisions. The Court relied by analogy on Chandi Prasad Chokhani v. State of Bihar, which cautioned against proceedings that could produce conflicting decisions.

predicates.civil_revision_followed_by_writ: A party first sought revision of a subordinate court’s order in a civil proceeding and later brought a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.revision_remedy_chosen_and_exhausted: The party chose revision as a means of challenging the order, and the revision proceeding ended without granting the requested relief.
predicates.later_writ_attacks_same_order: The later writ proceeding challenges the same order that was the subject of the revision.

issues.definition: When a party brings a writ proceeding against the same order after choosing and exhausting revision without obtaining relief, relief in the later writ proceeding is refused as improper.
